title: The Heroine of Dada and the Wulffschule: Hamburg, the Mountain, and Sixty-Nine Years in Basel
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Hamburg, born on the last day of August
stops.date_confidence: attested: German Wikipedia, 'Katja Wulff', gives 31 August 1890 at Hamburg, and Wikidata Q43267718 the same.
stops.campa: A daughter is born in Hamburg to Hugo Friedrich Wulff and Marie Elisabetha Amalia Wulff, born Döring, on the last day of August 1890. The city around her is a port of the German Empire: brick warehouses, water, shipping offices, a bourgeois household that trains its girls in drawing and deportment. She leaves it at twenty-five and never lives in Germany again. In the paperwork she is Katja in some places and Käthe in others. Both spellings follow her through the catalogues for the next hundred and two years.
suggested_refs: Hamburg civil registration, 31 August 1890

stops.name: Hamburg, the drawing and gymnastics teacher
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years 1912-1915 by German Wikipedia, 'Katja Wulff'; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. The research pool's claim of a Gewerbeschule and of diplomas in 1912 and 1914 is not in that source and is not carried here: the Cologne finding aid that might hold it, faust.sk-kultur.de object 111, returns HTTP 404.
stops.campa: She trains as a Zeichen- und Turnlehrerin, a teacher of drawing and gymnastics, and takes up the post. For four years she stands in Hamburg classrooms correcting perspective in the morning and counting bodies through exercises in the afternoon. It is respectable salaried work for an unmarried woman of the Kaiserreich. The training is in two things at once, the eye that measures a line and the discipline that moves a body on command, and nobody in the building calls either of them art. The service record runs 1912 to 1915, and that is the whole of what is known about her four years in it.
suggested_refs: Hamburg school service records, 1912-1915

stops.name: Hamburg, the lesson with Gertrud Falke
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1913/14 by German Wikipedia, 'Katja Wulff'; exact month unknown, set to 01. The lifelong correspondence and shared photograph album with Falke come from the Cologne finding-aid description and could not be verified.
stops.campa: Gertrud Falke, one of two dancer sisters in Hamburg, takes her as a pupil. What Falke teaches is not ballet: it is the new German dance, movement generated out of the body's own impulse rather than from a codified vocabulary handed down from Paris and Milan. Wulff is twenty-three and already employed; she comes to it as an adult, out of the gymnasium rather than off the stage. The friendship outlasts the lessons. Letters and a shared photograph album run between the two women for decades afterward.
suggested_refs: Gertrud and Ursula Falke, the Hamburg dancer sisters

stops.name: Monte Verità, the summer course above Ascona
stops.date_confidence: attested to summer 1914 by German Wikipedia, 'Katja Wulff'; month and day set to order the segment. The course is named there only as a Ferienkurs at Rudolf von Laban's Schule für Kunst; the title 'Tanz, Ton, Wort' belongs to Laban's later Zürich teaching and is not attested for the 1914 Ascona course, so it is not used. Coordinate inherited from the atlas pin for Monte Verità.
stops.campa: She comes south to the hill above Ascona where Rudolf von Laban keeps his summer school on the vegetarian colony's land. The teaching is done barefoot on grass. Laban is building a grammar of human movement from nothing, in the open, with students arriving from six countries and sleeping in huts among the fruit trees. Johann Adam Meisenbach photographs the group that season by Lago Maggiore, not Lake Lugano as the later captions have it, and in one much-reproduced frame the figure standing on the slope in the orange dress is Wulff.
suggested_refs: Johann Adam Meisenbach's photographs of the Laban group at Ascona, 1914
Wulff's Monte Verità student card
sources: stadtgeschichtebasel.ch, 'Eine Avantgardistin auf Schritt und Tritt'

stops.name: Monte Verità, the box on the hillside
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The anecdote is carried by Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: an Extraordinary Life (2008), p. 35, and repeated in secondary Wulff writing; no contemporaneous document supporting it was found, and Preston-Dunlop's original English sentence was not seen, only a French rendering. Date set to order the segment.
stops.campa: The tradition holds that she walked to the mountain with a rucksack and no money at all, and that once there she made herself a shelter out of a large wooden storage box and lived in it through the season. Nothing written at the time says so. What is certain is that she stayed, that she was twenty-three, that she had left a salaried teaching post in a north German city, and that the colony fed and housed its people on almost nothing. Whether anybody on that hill ever saw the box, no document reached here can say.
stops.quote: a marché, avec son sac à dos, jusqu'au Monte Verità sans argent. Là elle s'est fait un abri primitif dans une grande boite de rangement et survit comme cela à la saison
stops.quote_source: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: an Extraordinary Life (Alton: Dance Books, 2008), p. 35, in the French rendering given by K. Montabord, 'Corps, lieux, appartenances'
suggested_refs: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: an Extraordinary Life (2008)

stops.name: Ascona, the war scatters the colony
stops.date_confidence: the outbreak and the scattering of the colony are attested and are dated 1914-08-01 in ida_hoffmann.journey.json and laban.journey.json; that Wulff was still on the hill when it happened is reconstruction, since neither file names her.
stops.campa: War is declared while the course is running. The students are subjects of the nations now mobilizing, and within days the international body of dancers on the hill comes apart: the Germans north to their call-up, the French west, the colony that had been an argument against nations emptied by them inside a week. Wulff is a German subject in Switzerland with a teaching post waiting for her, and she goes back to Hamburg and to the classroom. She has had one summer of it. She teaches the autumn term, and the year after that one too.
suggested_refs: The dispersal of the Monte Verità colony, August 1914

stops.name: Hamburg, the last salaried year
stops.date_confidence: attested: German Wikipedia gives 1912-1915 for the Hamburg teaching, so 1915 is its closing year. Month and day set to 01.
stops.campa: For one more year she stands in front of Hamburg schoolchildren, correcting perspective and counting exercises. Germany is at war, the coast is under blockade, and the profession she trained for is exactly as secure as it was before the shooting started. She gives it up anyway. In 1916 she crosses into neutral Switzerland to become a student again at twenty-six, in a discipline with no degrees anyone recognizes and no companies hiring. Her family's view of the decision is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: Hamburg teaching service, closing year 1915

segments.name: Zürich, the School and the Drums

stops.name: Zürich, entering Laban's Schule für Bewegungskunst
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1916 by German Wikipedia, 'Katja Wulff', with study under Laban and Mary Wigman; month and day set to 01. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from laban.journey.json, 'Zurich, the wartime school'.
stops.campa: Laban has moved his school to Zürich for the duration of the war, and Wulff enrolls in it. Mary Wigman is the assistant and the senior body in the room; Suzanne Perrottet teaches the music side. The training is pedagogy as much as performance, and it works toward a diploma in dance gymnastics and art dance. Wigman has been in the room two years longer than she has. Zürich in 1916 is the only city in Europe where a German, a Frenchwoman and a Hungarian can stand in the same studio without any of them being arrested for standing in it.
suggested_refs: Laban's Schule für Bewegungskunst, Zürich, 1915-1919

stops.name: Cabaret Voltaire, Spiegelgasse 1: the drums
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The date and coordinate are the shared atlas pin used by laban.journey.json and suzanne_perrottet.journey.json, both of which name Käthe Wulff among the Laban dancers drawn into the cabaret's orbit. German Wikipedia's article 'Dada' does not name her, which is a real limit on the attestation.
stops.campa: Five doors from Lenin's lodging, Hugo Ball's cabaret runs its evenings, and Laban's students walk down the hill to dance in them. Sophie Taeuber goes, and Suzanne Perrottet goes, and Wulff goes. Wulff has been studying dance for barely two years. The masks are Marcel Janco's, painted cardboard that fixes a face and forces the whole body to carry the expression instead. Perrottet plays Schoenberg and Satie at the piano, in a low room off the Spiegelgasse, to an audience that finds the sound hideous.
suggested_refs: Cabaret Voltaire, Spiegelgasse 1
Marcel Janco masks
sources: Hugo Ball, Flight Out of Time
Colegio Invisible atlas: laban.journey.json, suzanne_perrottet.journey.json (shared pin)

stops.name: Zürich, the letter about the hair
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1917 by stadtgeschichtebasel.ch, 'Eine Avantgardistin auf Schritt und Tritt', which quotes the letter only as a fragment, cut off mid-word at its opening. Month and day set to 01; the letter's place of writing is not stated and the Zürich school pin is used.
stops.campa: She cuts her hair off and writes to her sister about it. The letter survives only as a fragment, beginning in the middle of a word, and what is left of it is a defence: she moves better without it, and the short hair suits a large part of what she is. In 1917 a woman cutting her hair short is a public statement whether she wants it to be one or not, and she is not arguing aesthetics with her sister, she is reporting a change to her family. What the sister wrote back is not in the papers.
stops.quote: runter ist; es ist sogar so, dass ich mich besser bewege. Ausserdem geht das kurze Haar, so wie ich es nun trage, gut zu einem grossen Teil meines Wesens.
stops.quote_source: Katja Wulff to her sister, 1917, quoted in 'Eine Avantgardistin auf Schritt und Tritt: die Tänzerin und Tanzpädagogin Katja Wulff', Stadt.Geschichte.Basel
suggested_refs: The 1917 letter to her sister, quoted in fragment only
sources: stadtgeschichtebasel.ch, 'Eine Avantgardistin auf Schritt und Tritt'

stops.name: Galerie Dada, Bahnhofstrasse: the masks again
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the date and coordinate are the pin already used by mary_wigman.journey.json for the Galerie Dada soirées, where Käthe Wulff is named among the Laban dancers who crossed over. No programme naming her individually was located.
stops.campa: The cabaret has become a gallery two streets from the school, above a confectioner's on the Bahnhofstrasse, and the traffic between the two houses runs both ways. Mary Wigman drills the bodies in the studio; Dada borrows them in the evening. Wulff dances in Janco's masks while Ball and Tzara take the word apart at the lectern. Nobody at that lectern and nobody on that floor is asking what a movement is supposed to represent. No programme from these evenings names her on her own.
suggested_refs: Sophie Taeuber dancing in a Janco mask at the Galerie Dada, 1917 (photograph)
sources: Hugo Ball, Flight Out of Time (diary, 1917)

stops.name: Monte Verità, Sang an die Sonne
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as regards Wulff. The festival itself is attested for the night of 18 August 1917 at the close of the Anational Congress, and the date and coordinate are inherited from laban.journey.json. Later scholarship names Wulff among Laban's Monte Verità dancers, but no cast list giving her a role was located; she is documented in Laban's circle throughout 1917.
stops.campa: Laban stages the whole night on the mountain: the sun going down danced at evening on the meadow, demons at midnight before a grotto in the hillside, a choir at dawn to meet the sun coming up again. Mary Wigman dances it with torches at the close of a congress of pacifists and occultists, in the third year of the war. Whether Wulff is among the bodies on the grass that night the record does not say, and the scholars who put her there are reasoning from the company she kept in the two years around it.
suggested_refs: Sang an die Sonne, 1917 photographs

stops.name: Zürich, the diploma
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1918 by German Wikipedia, 'Katja Wulff', in tänzerisches Turnen und Kunsttanz; month and day set to 01.
stops.campa: She is certified: tänzerisches Turnen und Kunsttanz, dance gymnastics and art dance, signed out of Laban's school. In 1918 there is no state examination for any of this, no conservatory, no ministry; the diploma is worth exactly what the name at the bottom of it is worth, and Laban's name is beginning to be worth a great deal. She is twenty-seven, she has been at this four years, and the certificate licenses her to open a school of her own anywhere in the German-speaking world. She opens one in Basel in 1923.
suggested_refs: Wulff's 1918 Laban-school diploma, Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln

stops.name: Zürich, the Schule für Eurythmie with Perrottet
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, not resolved: German Wikipedia dates the founding 1918, while suzanne_perrottet.journey.json dates it September 1919 and calls its own date inferred. Neither is hard-attested to the month. Dated here to 1918 with month and day set to 01; the coordinate is Perrottet's own pin for the school.
stops.campa: She and Suzanne Perrottet open a school together and call it a Schule für Eurythmie, which turns out to be a mistake of naming rather than of substance. Rudolf Steiner's anthroposophical movement has claimed the word for an entirely different discipline, and the two women spend years explaining what they are not before the thing is renamed. The partnership does not last long. Perrottet keeps the school and teaches in Zürich for the rest of her working life, and Wulff goes to Italy. When Perrottet dictates her recollections onto tape in her nineties, Wulff is in them.
suggested_refs: Schule für Eurythmie, Zürich, later the Bewegungsschule Suzanne Perrottet
sources: Colegio Invisible atlas: suzanne_perrottet.journey.json (shared pin, conflicting date)

stops.name: Kaufleuten, Pelikanstrasse 18: the red paper bag
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The episode rests on Hans Arp's memoir 'Dadaland', in Unsern täglichen Traum (Zürich: Arche, 1955), written some thirty-six years after the fact and not retrieved here; German Wikipedia's article 'Dada' mentions neither Wulff nor a paper bag nor a Kaufleuten evening. The Historisches Lexikon der Schweiz article 044712, cited elsewhere as independent corroboration of the phrase, returns HTTP 403 and could not be read. The eighth Dada soirée at the Kaufleuten is dated 9 April 1919 and the hall stands at Pelikanstrasse 18, correcting the research pool's Talstrasse coordinate.
stops.campa: The eighth Dada evening fills the Kaufleuten hall, and the evening turns. Wulff reads Arp's poems from underneath a large fiery-red paper bag that covers her head and shoulders, so that what the audience is being shouted at by is a bag. When part of that audience gets up and moves toward her she keeps reading. She is twenty-eight. Arp, writing it down thirty-six years later, gives her the two words that most books mentioning her at all will quote: Heldin Dadas, the heroine of Dada.
stops.quote_source: Hans (Jean) Arp, 'Dadaland', in Unsern täglichen Traum (Zürich: Arche, 1955), as quoted in stadtgeschichtebasel.ch, 'Eine Avantgardistin auf Schritt und Tritt'
suggested_refs: Hans Arp, 'Dadaland', in Unsern täglichen Traum (1955)
The Kaufleuten Festsaal, Pelikanstrasse 18, Zürich
sources: stadtgeschichtebasel.ch, 'Eine Avantgardistin auf Schritt und Tritt'

stops.name: Zürich, teaching the twelve-year-old
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Vera Skoronel's entry into the Zürich school under Perrottet and Wulff is dated to Easter 1919 by vera_skoronel.journey.json and to 1919-04-01 by engelmann.journey.json; the pin and the 20 April date are inherited byte-identical from the former, and the month and day should be read as approximate.
stops.campa: A twelve-year-old named Vera Skoronel is brought to the school and put into Wulff's hands and Perrottet's. Wulff is twenty-eight and three years out of her own training, and she is already the veteran of the room: the one who was on the mountain and who holds the diploma. Skoronel will be dead at twenty-six with a company and a reputation behind her. Two separate records date the girl's arrival to Easter 1919. Neither says a word about what she was given to do in her first term.
suggested_refs: The Laban school of Zurich under Suzanne Perrottet and Käthe Wulff, 1919
sources: Colegio Invisible atlas: vera_skoronel.journey.json (shared pin), engelmann.journey.json

stops.name: Amalfi, three years on the coast
stops.date_confidence: circa. German Wikipedia gives only 'drei Jahre lang' on the Amalfi coast and Capri, with no years at all; the span is inferred from the 1918 diploma and the 1923 Basel founding, and the date here orders the segment. The research pool's Italian residence certificates of 1921 and 1923 appear in no source reached.
stops.campa: She leaves Switzerland and goes south. For roughly three years she teaches dance on the Amalfi coast, in a country that had been at war with the country of her birth until the year before and where nobody has heard of Laban. No school of hers from these years is named in any record, no pupil, no address, no performance. What survives is the fact of the three years and the fact that she went alone. She is twenty-eight when she goes and the Zürich correspondence stops here.
suggested_refs: The Amalfi coast, c. 1919-1922

stops.name: Capri, the island lessons
stops.date_confidence: circa; the Capri period is attested by German Wikipedia without any dates and is placed here inside the inferred Italian span. Month and day order the segment and are not evidence.
stops.campa: Capri in the early twenties holds a floating population of foreigners living cheaply on a rock: Germans, Russians, English, painters and invalids and people avoiding somewhere. Wulff teaches dance among them. It is the least documented stretch of her hundred and two years, and the only one in which she is attached to no institution, no teacher, and no school of her own. Nobody records what she taught, or in what room, or to whom, or in which language. She is thirty when it ends and she goes north.

stops.name: Basel, founding the Wulffschule
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1923 by German and English Wikipedia; month and day set to 01. The school's street address in its first years was not established from any source reached, and the coordinate is central Basel.
stops.campa: She settles in Basel and opens a school for Ausdruckstanz, called in the advertisements the Basler Labanschule and by everybody else the Wulffschule. The choice of city is practical: Zürich, Bern and Geneva already have free-dance schools and Basel does not. She is thirty-two, teaching under the name of her own master because the name sells, and running the first thing in her life that belongs to her. Two of her posters survive in a Leipzig collection, advertising Körperbildung and Bewegungskunst.
suggested_refs: Posters 'Körperbildung, Bewegungskunst, Labanschule Käthe Wulff', Plakatsammlung Tanzarchiv Leipzig, NL 408/1608 and NL 408/1609
sources: Kalliope listing for the Leipzig poster collection (not re-verifiable: search endpoint returned HTTP 400)

stops.name: Basel, Tanzstudio Wulff
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1926 by German and English Wikipedia for the studio and for the Sacher, Bill and Oppenheim collaboration; month and day set to 01. The Glauser dedication is catalogued in the Cologne finding aid per the research pool; that finding aid returns HTTP 404 and the poem's text is reproduced nowhere reached.
stops.campa: The school grows a performing arm. Tanzstudio Wulff takes the best of the pupils onto a stage, with Mariette von Meyenburg choreographing most of the repertory and Wulff directing the company. From this year her Basel circle widens past dance: the conductor Paul Sacher, Max Bill, Meret Oppenheim. Friedrich Glauser, a morphine addict who is writing the crime novels that will make his name, hands her a poem with a dedication on it in his own hand. The archive that holds the sheet does not reproduce the poem.
stops.quote_source: Friedrich Glauser, handwritten dedication on a poem, 1926, catalogued in the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln finding aid, Nachlass Katja Wulff
suggested_refs: Friedrich Glauser's dedicated poem, 1926, Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln

stops.name: Stadttheater Basel, barefoot on the institutional stage
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The date and the Casella and Rieti programme are carried from background material said to derive from Basel city-history and Tanzarchiv programme records; none of it was independently retrieved. Only the Sacher collaboration from 1926 is independently attested, by German Wikipedia. The coordinate is the Steinenberg site of the Stadttheater that stood from 1875 to 1975, correcting the research pool's 47.5556/7.5886, which lands near Barfüsserplatz.
stops.campa: The company is given the city's own theatre. The programme is group and solo dances to music by Alfredo Casella, with Paul Sacher conducting his chamber orchestra, and then Barabau, a ballet to Vittorio Rieti. Wulff is thirty-six and four years into her own school. A Basel subscription audience that has watched ballet in that house for fifty years sits through an expressionist vocabulary arriving on a municipal stage with the municipal orchestra in the pit behind it. The dancers come out barefoot on the boards.
suggested_refs: Programme of the Tanzstudio Wulff evening, Stadttheater Basel, 27 February 1927

stops.name: Magdeburg, the congress in question
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, not resolved, and kept as reconstruction rather than deleted. A congress card and a photograph of the Wulffschule's exhibition stand at the Magdeburg Deutscher Tänzerkongress of 1927 are claimed from the Cologne finding aid, which returns HTTP 404; German Wikipedia dates Wulff's congress appearances '1928 bis 1930', which excludes 1927. The Kalliope record cited in support, DE-611-BF-120807, says nothing about Magdeburg. Month and day set to 01.
stops.campa: The first German dancers' congress meets at Magdeburg to decide what the new dance is for, and whether it is one thing or several. Whether Wulff is in the hall is precisely what the sources disagree about. A congress card and a photograph of her school's exhibition stand are said to be in her papers at Cologne; the German biographical summary of her life begins her congress attendance a year later. Both cannot be right, and the finding aid that would settle it is offline.
suggested_refs: Erster Deutscher Tänzerkongress, Magdeburg, 1927

stops.name: Essen, the dancers' congress
stops.date_confidence: attested: German Wikipedia gives 1928 to 1930 for Wulff's appearances at the German dancers' congresses, and the second congress met at Essen in 1928. Month and day set to 01. The lecture manuscript itself is a finding-aid claim and could not be checked.
stops.campa: At Essen the argument has moved on from what the new dance is to who owns it, and the congress is thick with schools defending their methods. Wulff comes from Basel with a lecture manuscript on dance pedagogy, and the studio performs inside the programme. She is by now a foreign delegate to a German conversation: her school is Swiss, her training is Laban's, her passport is still German. The papers from Essen go into her fonds and are in Cologne today.
suggested_refs: Zweiter Deutscher Tänzerkongress, Essen, 1928

stops.name: Bern, the Viererfeld: SAFFA
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1928 by German Wikipedia; the exhibition ran 26 August to 30 September 1928 on the Viererfeld in the Länggasse-Felsenau quarter, per German Wikipedia, 'Schweizerische Ausstellung für Frauenarbeit'. The opening date places the stop. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's Bern city centre.
stops.campa: The first Swiss exhibition for women's work covers the Viererfeld with pavilions counting up what women in this country actually do: nursing, teaching, farming, textiles, office work, and one dance school from Basel run by a German woman who is not yet a citizen. Wulff shows the Wulffschule there and keeps the participation certificate among her papers. The exhibition runs five weeks and closes at the end of September. Swiss women will not have the federal vote for another forty-three years.
suggested_refs: SAFFA I, Viererfeld, Bern, 26 August to 30 September 1928

stops.name: Munich, the last congress
stops.date_confidence: attested: German Wikipedia gives 1928 to 1930 for the congress appearances, and the third Deutscher Tänzerkongress met at Munich in 1930. Month and day set to 01. The participant card and school-director questionnaire are claimed from the Cologne finding aid, which could not be opened.
stops.campa: Munich holds the third congress and the last one. She has been crossing the border to these meetings for three years, arguing method with people who run schools like hers in cities she chose not to work in, and coming back each time to a school that is hers alone. After 1930 no travel of hers into Germany appears in the record again. What she brought home to Basel from Munich went into the boxes and is there now: a participant's card, and a questionnaire for school directors filled in by hand.
suggested_refs: Dritter Deutscher Tänzerkongress, Munich, 1930

stops.name: Bern, Hyspa
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Wulffschule's participation in Hyspa, the Swiss hygiene and sport exhibition, is carried from the Cologne finding aid via the research pool and was not independently confirmed; faust.sk-kultur.de object 111 returns HTTP 404. The exhibition grounds were not located and the coordinate is central Bern. Month and day set to 01.
stops.campa: Hyspa is the national exhibition of hygiene and sport, and the Wulffschule takes a place in it. This is where the free-dance schools of the twenties actually made their living: not in theatres but inside the public argument about bodies, breathing, posture, the well-run citizen. Wulff had trained as a gymnastics teacher in Hamburg before she ever saw Ascona, and had taught school exercises for four years before that training led anywhere. What the school put in its stand, and what was demonstrated on the floor of it, is described in nothing that can be read.
suggested_refs: Hyspa, Schweizerische Ausstellung für Hygiene und Sport, Bern, 1931
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln finding aid, via the research dossier (not opened: HTTP 404)

stops.name: Zürich, the Stadttheater guest engagement
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. A guest-performance contract with the Stadttheater Zürich for 1931/32 is described in the Cologne finding aid per the research pool; the finding aid could not be opened. Month and day order the segment. The coordinate is the Sechseläutenplatz building, the Stadttheater of the period and today's Opernhaus, correcting the research pool's 47.3656/8.5427; OpenStreetMap's first Opernhaus hit at 47.3892/8.5188 is the Schiffbau annex and is not used.
stops.campa: Tanzstudio Wulff signs to appear at the Zürich Stadttheater, and Wulff comes back to the city she trained in as the director of a company rather than as somebody else's student. Twelve years have passed since the Kaufleuten evening and the founding of the eurythmy school. What was danced under the contract is recorded nowhere; the contract itself sits in her papers at Cologne, filed with everything else she kept. Suzanne Perrottet is in the city that season too, still teaching a few streets from the theatre.
suggested_refs: Guest-performance contract, Stadttheater Zürich, 1931/32
sources: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln finding aid, via the research dossier (not opened: HTTP 404)

stops.name: Basel, ninety-two letters to Rudolf Jakob Humm
stops.date_confidence: the friendship is attested: German Wikipedia states she befriended Rudolf Jakob Humm. The counts of 92 letters, 62 postcards and 2 telegrams, the run to 1977 and the signature Nachl R J Humm 93.30 at the Zentralbibliothek Zürich come from a Kalliope catalogue record that could not be re-fetched, the search endpoint returning the homepage or HTTP 400 on every query form. The stop is pinned in Basel, where she wrote from, not at the repository. Month and day set to 01.
stops.campa: She writes to the Zürich novelist Rudolf Jakob Humm and keeps writing for forty-five years, on into the 1970s and past his death, when the letters go on to his widow Lili. Ninety-two letters, sixty-two postcards, two telegrams, all of them catalogued now in the Zentralbibliothek Zürich under his name rather than under hers. It is the largest body of her own prose surviving anywhere in the world, and not a line of it has been edited or published. The run begins in 1932 and ends in 1977.
suggested_refs: Zentralbibliothek Zürich, Nachl R J Humm 93.30, letters from Katja Wulff, 1932-1977
sources: Kalliope catalogue listing (not re-verifiable: search endpoint returned HTTP 400)

stops.name: Basel, Club 33
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Wulff's and Vaucher's frequenting of Basel's Club 33 is carried from Basel city-history material via the research pool; the venue's address was not established and the coordinate is central Basel. German Wikipedia independently attests her collaboration with Max Bill and Meret Oppenheim from 1926, which situates her in these circles. Month and day set to 01.
stops.campa: Gruppe 33 forms in Basel in the year Hitler takes power in the country Wulff was born in: artists organizing against fascism across the river from Germany, Max Sulzbachner, Meret Oppenheim, the architects Paul Artaria and Hans Schmidt. Wulff and Charles Ferdinand Vaucher, the actor and dancer she is living with, are in the room. Vaucher carries a Communist Party card. She is a German national running a school in a Swiss border city, fifteen minutes' walk from Germany. She holds the German passport three more years.
suggested_refs: Gruppe 33 and Club 33, Basel
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Katja Wulff' (Bill and Oppenheim collaboration)
Basel city-history material, via the research dossier

stops.name: Basel, the naturalization
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1936 by German and English Wikipedia, with municipal citizenship in Basel; month and day set to 01.
stops.campa: She takes Swiss citizenship with municipal citizenship in Basel, thirteen years after arriving in the city and twenty-one years after leaving Hamburg. In 1936 a German woman in Basel exchanging a German passport for a Swiss one is doing something with more than administrative content in it. From that year she is legally of the place where her school stands. Of her reasons the record gives nothing at all: no statement, no application, no interview, no witness.
suggested_refs: Basel Bürgerrecht, 1936

stops.name: Basel, marrying Vaucher
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, not resolved: German Wikipedia gives 1939 and English Wikipedia gives 1937 for a marriage that followed years of unmarried cohabitation. Dated here to 1939 with month and day set to 01. A direct fetch of a German Wikipedia article on Vaucher himself returned HTTP 404, so his own page could not be used to break the tie.
stops.campa: After years of living together unmarried, which in Basel in the thirties is itself a position, she marries Charles Ferdinand Vaucher: actor, dancer, director, later a cabaret artist, and a Communist Party member. She is in her late forties and has run her own school for a decade and a half. The sources cannot agree on the year, one saying 1937 and another 1939, and there is no way visible from here to choose between them, so the marriage runs either eight years or ten. It ends in 1947.
suggested_refs: Basel civil registry, marriage to Charles Ferdinand Vaucher

stops.name: Zürich, the Landesausstellung
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1939 by German Wikipedia; the Swiss National Exhibition ran from May to October 1939, and the month and day here order the segment rather than dating the performance.
stops.campa: The Landesausstellung of 1939 is Switzerland showing itself to itself with a war visible from every border, and the school and the company perform inside it. Wulff has been in the country sixteen years and a citizen for three. A dance school founded by a German woman in Basel is now part of the display of what the country is, exhibited beside the farming and the watchmaking and the army. The exhibition opens in May and closes in October. Poland has been invaded a month before that, and the Swiss army is mobilized while the pavilions are still open.
suggested_refs: Schweizerische Landesausstellung, Zürich, 1939

stops.name: Basel, the divorce
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1947 by German and English Wikipedia; month and day set to 01.
stops.campa: The marriage to Vaucher ends. She is fifty-six, she has been in Basel for twenty-four years, and the school has run through the whole war in a country ringed by it without closing a term: through the mobilization of 1939, through the rationing, through the years when the frontier a quarter of an hour from her studio was the edge of the Reich. Nothing in the reachable record says why the marriage ended, or which of them wanted it to, or where Vaucher went afterward. The record has the year of the decree. The school's terms run on through it without a break.
suggested_refs: Basel civil registry, divorce, 1947

stops.name: Basel, Augustinergasse 3
stops.date_confidence: the address is attested by German Wikipedia, which quotes the memorial plaque verbatim; the year she moved in is not. The commonly repeated 1947 is an inference from the divorce and appears in no source reached, so it orders the segment and is not evidence. Month and day set to 01. Coordinate is Augustinergasse 3 per OpenStreetMap, correcting two different wrong coordinates in the research pool.
stops.campa: She lives and teaches at Augustinergasse 3, on the Münsterhügel above the Rhine, in the oldest quarter of Basel, a few steps from the cathedral. The teaching happens in the flat, and she will be at this address another forty-five years. Pupils come up the stairs of a private house in a medieval lane for lessons in a discipline that was invented on a hill in Ticino while their parents were children, taught to them by a woman who was standing on that hill when it happened.
suggested_refs: Augustinergasse 3, Basel, Münsterhügel

stops.name: Basel, the philosophers' post
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to content. Kalliope lists postcards from Wulff to the Basel philosopher Paul Häberlin, 1948 to 1953, and correspondence with the historian and diplomat Carl Jacob Burckhardt, 1969 to 1970, both held at the Universitätsbibliothek Basel; neither set was read, and the Kalliope search endpoint could not be re-queried. The date orders the segment across both runs. The stop is pinned in Basel, where she wrote from.
stops.campa: Postcards go from her flat to Paul Häberlin, the Basel philosopher and psychologist, across five postwar years, and twenty years after that a correspondence runs with Carl Jacob Burckhardt, the historian who had been the League of Nations commissioner in Danzig. Both sets are catalogued in the university library under the men's names. She has never written a book and will not write one. What a dance teacher of seventy-nine and a former commissioner of Danzig found to say to each other in 1969, nobody has published.
suggested_refs: Universitätsbibliothek Basel, Wulff correspondence with Paul Häberlin (1948-1953) and Carl Jacob Burckhardt (1969-1970)
sources: Kalliope catalogue listings (not re-verifiable: search endpoint returned HTTP 400)

stops.name: Basel, the Arp opening
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. A photograph of Wulff by Maria Netter at a 1958 Hans Arp exhibition opening in Basel is listed in SIK-ISEA and Fotostiftung Schweiz material per the research pool and was not viewed; the venue is not established and the coordinate is central Basel. The Arp correspondence of 1935 to 1959 is described in the Cologne finding aid, which returns HTTP 404. Month and day set to 01.
stops.campa: Thirty-nine years after she read his poems out of a paper bag, Hans Arp has an exhibition opening in Basel and Wulff is in the room. She is sixty-seven and has been teaching in this city for thirty-five years. Maria Netter photographs her there, in a crowd, at an opening. The correspondence between them, and with Marguerite Arp, has run since the mid-thirties and will run one year more. Arp is among the last people alive who stood in the Kaufleuten hall that night, and it is his 1955 account of it, not hers, that the books use. He dies in 1966.
suggested_refs: Maria Netter's photograph of Katja Wulff at the Arp opening, Basel 1958, SIK-ISEA / Fotostiftung Schweiz
sources: SIK-ISEA / Fotostiftung Schweiz record, via the research dossier (not viewed)

stops.name: Basel, still teaching at ninety
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia, which states she was still actively teaching at her school at ninety; the Delpy recollection is quoted by German Wikipedia in German, and the wording carried here is an English translation of it, not the original. Month and day set to 01.
stops.campa: She is ninety and she is still taking classes in the flat at Augustinergasse 3, up the stairs, in the rooms where she also sleeps. The Wulffschule has by now taught Basel bodies for fifty-seven years, through a world war and a general mobilization, and what it teaches came off a hillside above Ascona in 1914, from Rudolf von Laban and from people who are almost all of them dead. A former pupil, Mary Delpy, remembers the dress: always very discreet, without ornament of any kind, and a gait that was almost regal.
stops.quote: Katja always dressed very discreetly... she had an almost regal gait
stops.quote_source: A dancer's recollection quoted in German Wikipedia, 'Katja Wulff'; carried here in English translation, the original German wording not seen
suggested_refs: Recollections of Wulffschule pupils, collected for the 2001 commemoration

stops.name: Basel, the interview with Raimund Meyer
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to place: the research pool gives 'Zürich or Basel' and the venue is not established, so the stop sits at her own Augustinergasse address. The interview is dated 1982 through Raimund Meyer, Dada in Zürich. Die Akteure, die Schauplätze (1990), pp. 97 and 99, quoted in French translation by K. Montabord, 'Corps, lieux, appartenances', which was verified directly; neither the 1990 volume nor the original German wording was retrieved, and the imprint is given as Luchterhand by Montabord and as Arche elsewhere. Month and day set to 01.
stops.campa: A Dada historian comes to interview her, sixty-three years after the Kaufleuten, and she declines the story he has come for. There was no link, she tells him, and no unified school: Zürich was small, artists met each other because everybody met everybody, and now and then they did something together. She went to Italy and it was finished. They never wrote to one another again and never met again. She is ninety-one. It was ephemeral, she tells him, and it was very good, and we took part.
stops.quote: Vous auriez aimé y voir un lien, mais il n'y en a pas. Le cercle de créateurs artistiques n'était pas bien grand à Zurich. On finit toujours par se rencontrer en général. [...] Nous ne nous sommes jamais réécrit. Nous ne nous sommes jamais revus. Je suis d'abord partie en Italie. Cette époque fut révolue. C'était quelque chose d'éphémère. Et c'était très bien. Nous avons participé.
stops.quote_source: Katja Wulff to Raimund Meyer, 1982, in Dada in Zürich. Die Akteure, die Schauplätze (1990), p. 97, in the French translation given by K. Montabord, 'Corps, lieux, appartenances'
suggested_refs: Raimund Meyer, Dada in Zürich. Die Akteure, die Schauplätze (1990), pp. 97 and 99
K. Montabord, 'Corps, lieux, appartenances', tristan.ube.fr

segments.name: The Hörnli, the Plaque, and the Archive

stops.name: Basel, Felix Platter-Spital
stops.date_confidence: attested: German and English Wikipedia both give 11 June 1992 at the Felix Platter-Spital. The age is contradicted between them and the contradiction is left open: German Wikipedia says 102, which its own birth date of 31 August 1890 contradicts, while English Wikipedia and the arithmetic give 101. Coordinate is the Burgfelderstrasse hospital in the St. Johann quarter per OpenStreetMap, correcting the research pool's 47.5735/7.6083, which lands in Kleinbasel on the wrong side of the Rhine.
stops.campa: She dies in the Felix Platter hospital on the eleventh of June 1992, eleven weeks short of her hundred and second birthday. The German notices say a hundred and two; the arithmetic from her own birth date gives a hundred and one, and the notices are wrong. She was born a subject of the German Empire and dies a Swiss citizen of Basel, having taught in the same city for sixty-nine years and at the same address for forty-five of them. The hospital stands on the Burgfelderstrasse, on the far side of Grossbasel from the Münsterhügel.
suggested_refs: Felix Platter-Spital, Burgfelderstrasse, Basel

stops.name: Friedhof am Hörnli, the urn
stops.date_confidence: attested as to place: German Wikipedia states the urn was interred at the Friedhof am Hörnli and carries a photograph of the grave; Wikidata Q43267718 gives the same place of burial. The interment date itself was not established and the month and day order the segment. Coordinate is Hörnliallee 70, Riehen, per OpenStreetMap; the research pool gave three different and all incorrect coordinates for this one cemetery, reconciled here.
stops.campa: The urn goes into the ground at the Hörnli, the municipal cemetery on the Riehen side of the city and the largest in Switzerland. A photograph of the grave exists, and it is the only image of it anybody has published. She had lived a hundred and one years, and the burial takes up one sentence in the record. Nothing about the marker is described in anything that can be read: not the stone, not the inscription, not who paid for the plot, not who stood at it.
suggested_refs: Friedhof am Hörnli, Hörnliallee 70, Riehen

stops.name: Augustinergasse 3, the plaque
stops.date_confidence: attested: the event of 23 June 2001 is documented on simonbaur.ch, '2001: Katja Wulff', by its co-organizer, and the plaque and its wording are quoted verbatim by German Wikipedia. This is a posthumous stop, staged at Wulff's own doorway and concerning her own memorial, nine years after her death.
stops.campa: Nine years after her death an initiative called Wer hat Katja Wulff tanzen gesehen? gathers at her doorway and puts the question in its own name. Several women standing in the lane answer it. The plaque goes up, photographs are exhibited, former pupils dance on the cobbles, and Bettina Zeugin's small illustrated book on her is launched the same afternoon, the only book about her that exists. The plaque reads: here lived and taught Katja Wulff, dancer and dance pedagogue.
stops.quote: Ja, wir haben Katja Wulff tanzen gesehen.
stops.quote_source: Dancers present at the commemorative event of 23 June 2001, organized by Simon Baur and Silvia Buol for IG Tanz Basel, simonbaur.ch/2001-katja-wulff
suggested_refs: The memorial plaque at Augustinergasse 3, Basel
Bettina Zeugin (ed.), Katja Wulff (Basel: IG Tanz Basel / Zwischen-Raum-Verlag, 2001), ISBN 3-909309-05-4

stops.name: Friedhof am Hörnli, the grave lifted
stops.date_confidence: attested by German Wikipedia, which states plainly 'Das Grab wurde 2022 aufgehoben'; the research pool carried this as unconfirmed tradition, but the article asserts it at the same evidentiary level as the rest of its biography. Caveat kept: this rests on Wikipedia and no cemetery register was consulted. Month and day set to 01.
stops.campa: In 2022, thirty years on, the plot at the Hörnli is cleared. Swiss cemeteries lift graves after a fixed lease unless a family renews the term, and nobody renewed this one. The grave of the woman Arp called the heroine of Dada is gone, and the cemetery photograph that is still published is a photograph of something that is not there. Whether anyone was asked before the plot was cleared is not recorded. No cemetery register was consulted for this, only the one encyclopedia sentence saying the grave was lifted.
suggested_refs: Friedhof am Hörnli, grave clearance, 2022

stops.name: Cologne, Deutsches Tanzarchiv: Bestand Nr. 014
stops.date_confidence: attested as to repository and reference: the Kalliope EAD record DE-611-BF-120807 confirms the Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, her profession and a Laufzeit of 1890 to 1978, and deutsches-tanzarchiv.de confirms Bestand Nr. 014. The extent figures of 28 boxes, 4 folders and 2 cartons, the icosahedron model, the four-part arrangement and the correspondence spans all come from the finding aid at faust.sk-kultur.de object 111, which returns HTTP 404 and could not be read. Wulff is not known to have visited Cologne; the date orders the segment and is not an event in her life. Coordinate is Im Mediapark 7, Neustadt-Nord, per OpenStreetMap, correcting the research pool's Altstadt coordinate.
stops.campa: Her papers are in Cologne, in the Media Park, as Bestand Nr. 014 of the German Dance Archive: correspondence, diplomas, school records, drawings, photographs, posters. The fonds runs from her birth year to 1978. The letters to Laban stop in 1957; those to Mary Wigman run from 1915 to 1954, thirty-nine years of a friendship begun in a wartime studio. Also in the boxes, listed among the objects, is a physical model of an icosahedron, Laban's solid, the twenty-sided figure he used to map the directions a body can move through space.
suggested_refs: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Nachlass Katja Wulff, Bestand Nr. 014, Kalliope DE-611-BF-120807
